extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public and essayists interested in manners, character-sketching, and moral/social observation
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and exemplars for composing short moral and social essays: how to observe and report manners, character, and anecdote so as to entertain and instruct. Emphasises characterisation, use of detail, and moral purpose in essayistic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dating portraits with contemporary fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Great Masters in Painting never care for drawing People in the Fashion; ... they often represent an illustrious Person in a Roman Habit, or in some other Dress that never varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ornament a portrait (or by extension a description) with transient accessories that will look 'monstrous in the Eyes of Posterity.' Prefer stable, conventional or timeless clothing/attributes to preserve dignity and avoid dating the work. Example given: painters putting illustrious persons in Roman habit instead of current headdresses/periwigs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide 'everlasting drapery' / avoid slavish following of fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: I could wish... that there was such a kind of everlasting Drapery to be made use of by all who live at a certain distance from the Town... For want of this standing Dress, a Man who takes a Journey into the Country is as much surprised... and finds as great a Variety of Garbs and Habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting country characters, avoid excessive emphasis on the latest town fashions; show constancy of habit as a virtue and a means to avoid becoming ridiculous. The essay suggests that fixed habits may occasionally coincide with fashion (clock metaphor): running after mode makes a character appear ridiculous and mutable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete, comic particulars of dress and manner to characterise/satirise
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter lists comic particulars (e.g., 'Her Commode was not half a Foot high, and her Petticoat within some Yards of a modish Circumference'; 'a young Fellow with a tolerable Periwig, had it not been covered with a Hat that was shaped in the Ramillie Cock').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select vivid, specific, often exaggerated details of costume, gesture, and domestic objects to create humour and social satire. The examples (commode height, scanty petticoats, flaxen periwigs, flounced garments) show how precise visual detail makes characters recognisable and amusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasise inner qualities over modes and apparel
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no ordinary Part of humane Life which expresseth so much a good Mind... as his Behaviour upon meeting with Strangers... 'Modes and Apparel are but Trifles to the real Man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral or character writing, foreground behaviour, manners, and disposition rather than outward fashion. Show moral worth through actions (kindness, courtesy, restraint) rather than relying on fashionable dress as the signifier of a person's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show good breeding by behaviour toward strangers and the humble
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no ordinary Part of humane Life which expresseth so much a good Mind, and a right inward Man, as his Behaviour upon meeting with Strangers... When two such as thee and I meet... thou should'st rejoice to see my peaceable Demeanour, and I should be glad to see thy Strength and Ability to protect me in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small social scenes—encounters on a coach, treatment of a beggar, courteous restraint—to reveal true character. Demonstrate humility, restraint, and a disposition to hide superiority as marks of goodness and breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ordinary social interactions and dialogue as material
rubrics_metrics.description: The Occurrences we met with were ordinary, and very little happened which could entertain by the Relation of them: But... the whole Journey was not spent in Impertinences... The Occurrences we met with were ordinary, and very little happened which could entertain by the Relation of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not invent grand incidents: ordinary events and the way people converse and behave provide rich material. Focus on dialogue, small quarrels, repartee, and the particulars of company to create interest and reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ anecdotes and illustrative stories to teach or exemplify morals
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall fill the remaining Part of my Paper with a Story... printed in one of our Monthly Accounts about twenty Years ago... the Merchant... found that he could speak readily in three or four Languages... the Boy proved to be the Son of the Merchant... the Lad was very well pleased to find a Father... the Father... delighted to see a Son return to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert self-contained tales (local stories, traveller's reports) that resolve with a moral or exemplify social truths (redemption, providence, virtue). Use concrete markers (moles, marks, languages) to make the anecdote credible and emotionally resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend contrasting virtues between characters to create harmonious portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: How different are the Lives of Aristus and Aspasia? the innocent Vivacity of the one is tempered and composed by the chearful Gravity of the other. The Wife grows wise by the Discourses of the Husband, and the Husband good-humour'd by the Conversations of the Wife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting relationships (marriage, family), balance opposing traits across characters so each improves or tempers the other; show the diffusion of virtues into the family as a unified moral atmosphere rather than isolating individual traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geography and social contrast (town vs. country) to illustrate characters and fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: As I proceeded in my Journey I observed the Petticoat grew scantier and scantier, and about threescore Miles from London was so very unfashionable... We fancied ourselves in King Charles the Second's Reign, the People having made very little Variations in their Dress since that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit regional differences to characterise people and to satirise or praise. Showing how fashion changes (or fails to reach) across distance gives social context and comic contrast; it's also a device to locate scenes and attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to both delight and improve the reader — combine entertainment with moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Paragraph is freight either with useful or delightful Notions... you charm the Fancy, sooth the Passions, and insensibly lead the Reader to that Sweetness of Temper... you rouse Generosity with that Spirit, and inculcate Humanity with that Ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for prose that amuses and instructs simultaneously: vary subjects, engage imagination, touch emotions, and subtly persuade readers toward generosity and humanity rather than preaching overtly. Variety and pleasant tone are instruments of moral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters, reports, and 'received' accounts as rhetorical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: I have received a Letter (which I there hinted at) from a Gentleman who is now in the Western Circuit... 'Sir, Being a Lawyer of the Middle-Temple, a Cornishman by Birth, I generally ride the Western Circuit for my health...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame material as letters, traveller's reports, or submissions from readers to introduce different voices, lend authenticity, and provide varied vantage points. Such devices let the author present multiple social scenes and exempla without direct assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restraint and humility in depictions of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: When he falleth in the way with Persons of Simplicity and Innocence, however knowing he may be in the Ways of Men, will not vaunt himself thereof; but will the rather hide his Superiority to them, that he may not be painful unto them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray superior characters as discreet and considerate rather than boastful; this behaviour is itself a mark of greatness and makes the depiction morally exemplary. Avoid representations that celebrate ostentation of knowledge or status.
